deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivations. It is a set of methodological and philosophical notebook entries that continue the previous page. That page discussed mathematics as 'experimenting with thoughts', transfinite principles such as the axiom of choice, and eliminating them from proofs of ordinary theorems.

(1) Continuing a sentence from the previous page, Hilbert says the application of 'my theory' (proof theory / axiomatic method) is 'another, more general, more spiritual' one. His method is meant to pull the ground from under 'those who deny everything except calculation' and who regard forming concepts as illegitimate. He calls them 'the Kroneckerian finiteness-fanatics'.

(2) A methodological maxim: 'Always strive to carry out a proof with the least elementary means.' The stated reason is that this best displays mastery of the subject and the governing idea. He marks this as the opposite of Weierstrass, Kronecker and their imitators, and adds that people call 'elementary' only what is familiar to them.

(3) A contrast between geometry and logic.
- In his Geometry (Grundlagen der Geometrie), points, lines and planes are only thought-things. They have nothing to do with real points, lines and planes.
- The logical signs 'or', 'and', 'not' are different. When we manipulate them as objects on paper, they also take on the meaning of the real 'or', 'not', 'and'. He calls this a 'piquancy' unique in science.
- In this way the logician 'experiments on paper', as the geodesist does in geometry and the experimenter in electricity theory. Logic is the region where coarse sensory empiricism and the purest thought flow into each other.
- This anticipates the finitary, sign-manipulating view of metamathematics in Hilbert's proof theory.

(4) A remark on physics. Why does temperature Θ have an absolute zero but time t does not? 'That is of course only due to the different axioms.' One could equally say of temperature, as of space and time, that it is a 'form of the understanding', since nothing is thinkable that does not happen at some temperature. This is a semi-ironic jab at Kantian a priori forms: the structure of a physical quantity is fixed by its axioms. It connects to the next page on axiomatizing heat conduction and the consistency of physical axioms (Neumann–Schwarz solvability of the boundary value problem).

No computations are present.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics on the page.

Philosophical looseness: in Kant, space and time are forms of intuition (Anschauungsformen), not forms of the understanding (Verstandesformen), whose a priori elements are the categories. Hilbert's 'Verstandesform' is imprecise, possibly deliberately ironic.

The claim that the difference between temperature and time with respect to an absolute zero lies 'only' in the axioms is a methodological stance, not a demonstrated result. Physically, absolute zero follows from thermodynamics (Kelvin scale, third law); it was not an arbitrary choice.

deep.surprise_reason: The page consists of well-known Hilbertian themes: anti-Kronecker polemic, the axiomatic and proof-theoretic program, and formulas as concrete objects one 'experiments' with. The Cod. Ms. Hilbert 600 notebooks have been mined by historians (Corry, Sieg, Rowe, Peckhaus). The phrasing of the maxim and the temperature/Kant remark are nice quotable details but carry no mathematical novelty.
